claim: The centromere is a specialized chromatin region marked by the histone H3 variant CENP-A.
source: The centromere is a specialized chromatin region marked by the histone H3 variant CENP-A.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centromere composition.

claim: Centromeric α-satellite transcription is dependent on RNA Polymerase II.
source: Here, we report that centromeric α-satellite transcription is dependent on RNA Polymerase II
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing transcription inhibition with α-amanitin (RNAPII inhibitor) reduces centromeric transcripts.

claim: Centromeric α-satellite transcription occurs at late mitosis into early G1.
source: Here, we report that centromeric α-satellite transcription is dependent on RNA Polymerase II and occurs at late mitosis into early G1
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data showing RNAPIIS2P localization at eG1 and transcription inhibition experiments at different cell cycle stages.

claim: The timing of centromeric transcription is concurrent with the timing of new CENP-A assembly.
source: occurs at late mitosis into early G1, concurrent with the timing of new CENP-A assembly
evidence: Based on known timing of CENP-A assembly and observed timing of transcription in this study.

claim: Inhibition of RNA Polymerase II-dependent transcription abrogates the recruitment of CENP-A to native human centromeres.
source: Inhibition of RNA Polymerase II-dependent transcription abrogates the recruitment of CENP-A and its chaperone HJURP to native human centromeres.
evidence: Supported by IF data showing ~50% decrease in CENP-A signal after α-amanitin treatment and chromatin fiber data showing loss of CENP-A.

claim: Inhibition of RNA Polymerase II-dependent transcription abrogates the recruitment of HJURP to native human centromeres.
source: Inhibition of RNA Polymerase II-dependent transcription abrogates the recruitment of CENP-A and its chaperone HJURP to native human centromeres.
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data showing loss of HJURP after α-amanitin treatment.

claim: CENP-A associated RNAs include a 1.3 kb molecule that originates from centromeres.
source: Biochemical characterization of CENP-A associated RNAs reveals a 1.3 kb molecule that originates from centromeres
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data showing a 1.3 kb band from CENP-A IP.

claim: The 1.3 kb centromeric RNA physically interacts with the soluble pre-assembly HJURP/CENP-A complex in vivo.
source: Biochemical characterization of CENP-A associated RNAs reveals a 1.3 kb molecule that originates from centromeres, which physically interacts with the soluble pre-assembly HJURP/CENP-A complex in vivo
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data showing the 1.3 kb RNA co-immunoprecipitates with CENP-A and HJURP from the soluble fraction.

claim: Down-regulation of the 1.3 kb centromeric RNA leads to the loss of CENP-A at centromeres.
source: whose down-regulation leads to the loss of CENP-A and HJURP at centromeres
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data showing loss of CENP-A after shRNA-mediated knockdown of centromeric transcripts.

claim: Down-regulation of the 1.3 kb centromeric RNA leads to the loss of HJURP at centromeres.
source: whose down-regulation leads to the loss of CENP-A and HJURP at centromeres
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data showing loss of HJURP after shRNA-mediated knockdown of centromeric transcripts.

claim: Human centromeric long non-coding RNAs have a novel function in the recruitment of HJURP and CENP-A.
source: This study describes a novel function for human centromeric long non-coding RNAs in the recruitment of HJURP and CENP-A
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data showing physical interaction of RNA with HJURP/CENP-A and loss of recruitment upon RNA depletion.

claim: RNA-based chaperone targeting is implicated in histone variant assembly.
source: implicating RNA-based chaperone targeting in histone variant assembly
evidence: Inferred from the data showing RNA interaction with HJURP and requirement for CENP-A loading.

claim: AT-rich 171 bp α-satellite repeats lacking any known genes are the primary DNA component of the human centromere.
source: In humans, AT-rich 171 bp α-satellite repeats lacking any known genes are the primary DNA component of the centromere (Waye and Willard, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waye and Willard, 1987.

claim: Centromeric chromatin exhibits a bivalent organization with heterochromatin-like post-translational modifications such as H3 and H4 hypo-acetylation.
source: Centromeric chromatin has long been considered heterochromatic, despite exhibiting a bivalent organization with heterochromatin-like post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as H3 and H4 hypo-acetylation, and transcription-coupled PTMs, including dimethylation on H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me2) (Sullivan and Karpen, 2004; Heintzman et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sullivan and Karpen, 2004; Heintzman et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Centromeric chromatin exhibits transcription-coupled PTMs including dimethylation on H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me2).
source: Centromeric chromatin has long been considered heterochromatic, despite exhibiting a bivalent organization with heterochromatin-like post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as H3 and H4 hypo-acetylation, and transcription-coupled PTMs, including dimethylation on H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me2) (Sullivan and Karpen, 2004; Heintzman et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sullivan and Karpen, 2004; Heintzman et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Chemical inhibition of RNA Polymerase I results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C.
source: Chemical inhibition of either RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI), or RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C, and in chromosome mis-segregation (Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012.

claim: Chemical inhibition of RNA Polymerase II results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C.
source: Chemical inhibition of either RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI), or RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C, and in chromosome mis-segregation (Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012.

claim: Chemical inhibition of RNA Polymerase I results in chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Chemical inhibition of either RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI), or RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C, and in chromosome mis-segregation (Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012.

claim: Chemical inhibition of RNA Polymerase II results in chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Chemical inhibition of either RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI), or RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), results in loss of the inner kinetochore protein CENP-C, and in chromosome mis-segregation (Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2012.

claim: Centromeric RNA components contribute to the structural integrity of the mitotic centromere.
source: Centromeric RNA components also seem to contribute to the structural integrity of the mitotic centromere (Wong et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2007.

claim: RNAPIIS2P co-localizes with the inner kinetochore protein CENP-B at eG1.
source: RNAPIIS2P co-localizes with the inner kinetochore protein CENP-B and centromeric α-satellite DNA specifically at eG1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RNAPIIS2P co-localizes with centromeric α-satellite DNA specifically at eG1.
source: RNAPIIS2P co-localizes with the inner kinetochore protein CENP-B and centromeric α-satellite DNA specifically at eG1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF/FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TBP is localized on eG1 CENP-A-rich fibers.
source: We also noted that TBP, a partner of RNAPII normally involved in transcription initiation (Vannini and Cramer, 2012), is localized on eG1 CENP-A-rich fibers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Vannini and Cramer, 2012.

claim: TBP is a partner of RNAPII normally involved in transcription initiation.
source: We also noted that TBP, a partner of RNAPII normally involved in transcription initiation (Vannini and Cramer, 2012), is localized on eG1 CENP-A-rich fibers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vannini and Cramer, 2012.

claim: Centromeres are actively transcribed by RNAPII machinery at eG1.
source: These data suggest that centromeres are actively transcribed by RNAPII machinery at eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization data of RNAPIIS2P and TBP with centromeric markers at eG1.

claim: RNAPII and TBP co-purify with CENP-A.
source: RNAPII and its partner TBP also co-purified with CENP-A and CENP-C (Figure 1B, left and middle panels).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from chromatin IP shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNAPII and TBP co-purify with CENP-C.
source: RNAPII and its partner TBP also co-purified with CENP-A and CENP-C (Figure 1B, left and middle panels).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from chromatin IP shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNAPII shows robust and reproducible binding to TBP.
source: While Western blots revealed little or no interaction of RNAPII with CENP-C, a robust and reproducible binding of RNAPII to TBP and CENP-A was observed (Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from RNAPIIS2P IP shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNAPII shows robust and reproducible binding to CENP-A.
source: While Western blots revealed little or no interaction of RNAPII with CENP-C, a robust and reproducible binding of RNAPII to TBP and CENP-A was observed (Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from RNAPIIS2P IP shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNAPII shows little or no interaction with CENP-C.
source: While Western blots revealed little or no interaction of RNAPII with CENP-C, a robust and reproducible binding of RNAPII to TBP and CENP-A was observed (Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from RNAPIIS2P IP shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Active RNAPII machinery is physically associated with CENP-A chromatin at eG1.
source: Thus, active RNAPII machinery is physically associated with CENP-A chromatin at eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the co-IP data showing RNAPII binding to CENP-A and TBP.

claim: RNAPII transcribes centromeres at mitosis.
source: Recent studies have indicated that RNAPII transcribes centromeres at mitosis (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2012.

claim: RNAPII inhibition in mitotic cells results in a 15.6% decrease in centromeric transcripts.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Chan et al., 2012), RNAPII inhibition in mitotic cells revealed a decrease (15.6%) in centromeric transcripts (Figure 2, right graph).
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 2 and citation to Chan et al., 2012.

claim: RNAPII inhibition in eG1 results in a 35.1% reduction in centromeric transcripts.
source: However, when RNAPII was blocked in eG1, a larger reduction (35.1%) was observed (Figure 2, right graph).
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: RNAPII transcribes centromeres throughout eG1.
source: These results suggest that RNAPII transcribes centromeres not solely at mitosis, but also throughout eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the transcription inhibition data showing greater reduction at eG1 than mitosis.

claim: CENP-B staining intensity is heterogeneous.
source: Consistent with its role as a constitutive centromeric DNA-binding protein (Verdaasdonk and Bloom, 2011), CENP-B staining intensity was heterogeneous (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by IF data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citation to Verdaasdonk and Bloom, 2011.

claim: CENP-B localization is independent of centromeric transcription.
source: but identical in both non-treated (NT) and α-amanitin-treated cells (Figure 3A,B; Supplementary file 1), demonstrating that its localization is independent of centromeric transcription.
evidence: Supported by IF quantification data showing no change in CENP-B signal after α-amanitin treatment.

claim: When RNAPII is blocked, the intensity of the CENP-A signal is decreased by approximately 50% in cells.
source: Whereas punctate CENP-A spots can be seen under both conditions, when RNAPII was blocked, the intensity of the CENP-A signal was decreased by ∼50% in cells (Figure 3A,B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 3A,B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: α-amanitin treatment does not change total levels of CENP-A protein.
source: To ensure that this decrease was not due to reduced expression of CENP-A or its chaperone HJURP, total levels of both proteins were quantified by Western blot. No noticeable changes in protein levels were detected upon α-amanitin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: α-amanitin treatment does not change total levels of HJURP protein.
source: To ensure that this decrease was not due to reduced expression of CENP-A or its chaperone HJURP, total levels of both proteins were quantified by Western blot. No noticeable changes in protein levels were detected upon α-amanitin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Equal amounts of CENP-A and HJURP are available at eG1 after α-amanitin treatment.
source: These data indicate that equal amounts of CENP-A and HJURP were available at eG1, but potentially unable to load at the centromere.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data showing no change in total protein levels.

claim: Inhibition of transcription does not affect RNAPIIS2P localization onto the centromeric fiber.
source: Consistent with the known effect of α-amanitin on RNAPII (i.e., blocking RNAPII elongation without inducing the release of RNAPII) (Nguyen et al., 1996; Bensaude, 2011), inhibition of transcription did not affect RNAPIIS2P localization onto the centromeric fiber (Figure 3C, first top panel).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Nguyen et al., 1996; Bensaude, 2011.

claim: α-amanitin blocks RNAPII elongation without inducing the release of RNAPII.
source: Consistent with the known effect of α-amanitin on RNAPII (i.e., blocking RNAPII elongation without inducing the release of RNAPII) (Nguyen et al., 1996; Bensaude, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 1996; Bensaude, 2011.

claim: CENP-B localization onto centromeric chromatin fibers remains unaffected after RNAPII inhibition.
source: Similarly, CENP-B localization onto centromeric chromatin fibers remained unaffected as well (Figure 3C, first panel).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After RNAPII inhibition, CENP-A signals are reduced on chromatin fibers.
source: Consistent with the whole cell data presented above (Figure 3A,B), after RNAPII inhibition, not only were CENP-A signals reduced on chromatin fibers (Figure 3C, second panel)
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After RNAPII inhibition, HJURP is almost completely lost from chromatin fibers.
source: after RNAPII inhibition, not only were CENP-A signals reduced on chromatin fibers (Figure 3C, second panel), HJURP was almost completely lost (Figure 3C, second panel).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RNAPII-dependent transcription is required for the targeting of HJURP to centromeric chromatin fiber at eG1.
source: The loss of HJURP (Figure 3C) combined with the ∼50% decrease of CENP-A signal after α-amanitin treatment (Figure 3B), suggests that RNAPII-dependent transcription is required for the targeting of HJURP, and for the subsequent loading of new CENP-A to the centromeric chromatin fiber at eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing loss of HJURP and reduced CENP-A after transcription inhibition.

claim: RNAPII-dependent transcription is required for the subsequent loading of new CENP-A to the centromeric chromatin fiber at eG1.
source: The loss of HJURP (Figure 3C) combined with the ∼50% decrease of CENP-A signal after α-amanitin treatment (Figure 3B), suggests that RNAPII-dependent transcription is required for the targeting of HJURP, and for the subsequent loading of new CENP-A to the centromeric chromatin fiber at eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing loss of HJURP and reduced CENP-A after transcription inhibition.

claim: No genes have been annotated within native human centromeres.
source: In humans, no genes have been annotated within native centromeres, suggesting a transcription event at α-satellite DNA repeats most likely leads to the synthesis of ncRNAs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of human centromere annotation.

claim: Transcription at α-satellite DNA repeats most likely leads to the synthesis of ncRNAs.
source: In humans, no genes have been annotated within native centromeres, suggesting a transcription event at α-satellite DNA repeats most likely leads to the synthesis of ncRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of annotated genes at centromeres.

claim: Northern blots revealed a unique centromeric RNA species migrating at approximately 1.3 kb.
source: Northern blots revealed a unique centromeric RNA species migrating at approximately ∼1.3 kb (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of RNA samples with RNase A demonstrates the absence of the 1.3 kb band on Northern blots.
source: Treatment of RNA samples with RNase A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), or purification of RNA from cells treated with α-amanitin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), both demonstrated the absence of the 1.3 kb band on Northern blots, supporting the interpretation that the 1.3 kb band derives solely from an RNA species.
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Purification of RNA from cells treated with α-amanitin demonstrates the absence of the 1.3 kb band on Northern blots.
source: Treatment of RNA samples with RNase A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), or purification of RNA from cells treated with α-amanitin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), both demonstrated the absence of the 1.3 kb band on Northern blots, supporting the interpretation that the 1.3 kb band derives solely from an RNA species.
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 1.3 kb band derives solely from an RNA species.
source: Treatment of RNA samples with RNase A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), or purification of RNA from cells treated with α-amanitin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), both demonstrated the absence of the 1.3 kb band on Northern blots, supporting the interpretation that the 1.3 kb band derives solely from an RNA species.
evidence: Inferred from the RNase A and α-amanitin treatment experiments.

claim: Computational RNA-binding prediction algorithms revealed potential RNA binding residues in HJURP.
source: Indeed, computational RNA-binding prediction algorithms revealed potential RNA binding residues in both HJURP and CENP-A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Computational RNA-binding prediction algorithms revealed potential RNA binding residues in CENP-A.
source: Indeed, computational RNA-binding prediction algorithms revealed potential RNA binding residues in both HJURP and CENP-A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: CENP-A and HJURP co-purify from both soluble fraction and chromatin fraction.
source: Consistent with HJURP chaperoning CENP-A at eG1 (Dunleavy et al., 2009; Foltz et al., 2009; Shuaib et al., 2010), these proteins co-purified from both SF and CF (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and citations to Dunleavy et al., 2009; Foltz et al., 2009; Shuaib et al., 2010.

claim: HJURP chaperones CENP-A at eG1.
source: Consistent with HJURP chaperoning CENP-A at eG1 (Dunleavy et al., 2009; Foltz et al., 2009; Shuaib et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunleavy et al., 2009; Foltz et al., 2009; Shuaib et al., 2010.

claim: The 1.3 kb RNA is physically associated with CENP-A in both soluble fraction and chromatin fraction.
source: In contrast, the 1.3 kb RNA is physically associated with CENP-A in both SF and CF (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data from CENP-A IP shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 1.3 kb RNA interacts with HJURP only in the soluble fraction.
source: and interacts with HJURP only in the SF (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data from HJURP IP shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 1.3 kb centromeric RNA physically associates with the soluble HJURP/CENP-A pre-assembly complex at eG1.
source: These data provide evidence that the 1.3 kb centromeric RNA physically associates with the soluble HJURP/CENP-A pre-assembly complex at eG1.
evidence: Inferred from the Northern blot data showing RNA co-IP with HJURP and CENP-A from soluble fraction.

claim: Cells transfected with shRNAscram displayed no changes in morphology and density.
source: Cells transfected with shRNAscram displayed no changes in morphology and density, whereas cells treated with shRNAcenRNA#1 displayed significant loss of cell density (down by ~70%, relative to control), and presented aberrant morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and 2B).
evidence: Supported by phase contrast microscopy and IF data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: Cells transfected with shRNAsat constructs displayed a significant decrease (approximately 70%) of the centromeric α-satellite transcript.
source: Compared to control shRNAscram, cells transfected with shRNAsat constructs displayed a significant decrease (∼70%) of the centromeric α-satellite transcript (Figure 6— figure supplement 1B), confirming targeted destruction was accomplished.
evidence: Supported by qtPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: shRNAsat-transfected cells were less dense (down by approximately 70%, relative to control).
source: Evaluation of cell morphology by phase contrast microscopy revealed that shRNAsat-transfected cells were less dense (down by ∼70%, relative to control) and exhibited abnormal morphology (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by phase contrast microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: shRNAsat-transfected cells exhibited abnormal morphology including a large and flat cytoplasm, cellular protrusions, and multinucleate cells.
source: Evaluation of cell morphology by phase contrast microscopy revealed that shRNAsat-transfected cells were less dense (down by ∼70%, relative to control) and exhibited abnormal morphology (Figure 6A). Phenotypes included a large and flat cytoplasm, cellular protrusions, and multinucleate cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by phase contrast microscopy and IF data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: No significant increase in senescence was seen in shRNAscram or shRNAsat-transfected cells.
source: However, no significant increase in senescence was seen in either shRNAscram or shRNAsat-transfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Almost half (42.2%) of shRNAsat-transfected cells presented abnormal mitoses, with multipolar spindles and lagging chromosomes.
source: In contrast, almost half (42.2%) of shRNAsat-transfected cells presented abnormal mitoses, with multipolar spindles and lagging chromosomes (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by IF data of mitotic cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In both shRNAscram- or shRNAsat-transfected cells, RNAPIIS2P remains associated with centromeric chromatin fibers.
source: In both, shRNAscram- or shRNAsat-transfected cells, RNAPIIS2P remains associated with centromeric chromatin fibers (Figure 7, first top panel), confirming that RNAPII localization and transcription of centromeres are independent of centromeric transcripts.
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: RNAPII localization and transcription of centromeres are independent of centromeric transcripts.
source: In both, shRNAscram- or shRNAsat-transfected cells, RNAPIIS2P remains associated with centromeric chromatin fibers (Figure 7, first top panel), confirming that RNAPII localization and transcription of centromeres are independent of centromeric transcripts.
evidence: Inferred from the chromatin fiber data showing RNAPIIS2P localization is maintained after centromeric transcript depletion.

claim: CENP-B localization was unaffected at centromeres in shRNAsat-transfected cells.
source: Additionally, CENP-B and CENP-C localization was also unaffected at centromeres (Figure 7, second and third panels).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: CENP-C localization was unaffected at centromeres in shRNAsat-transfected cells.
source: Additionally, CENP-B and CENP-C localization was also unaffected at centromeres (Figure 7, second and third panels).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: On centromeric fibers from shRNAsat-transfected cells, CENP-A was barely detectable.
source: In contrast, on centromeric fibers from shRNAsat-transfected cells, CENP-A and HJURP were barely detectable (Figure 7, fourth and fifth panels).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: On centromeric fibers from shRNAsat-transfected cells, HJURP was barely detectable.
source: In contrast, on centromeric fibers from shRNAsat-transfected cells, CENP-A and HJURP were barely detectable (Figure 7, fourth and fifth panels).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF data shown in Figure 7.

claim: At eG1, CENP-A targeting through its chaperone HJURP is dependent on the presence of centromeric transcripts.
source: These data suggest that at eG1, CENP-A targeting through its chaperone HJURP is dependent not just on active transcription itself, nor on processes that facilitate centromeric transcription (Barnhart et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014), but specifically requires the presence of centromeric transcripts.
evidence: Inferred from the chromatin fiber data showing loss of CENP-A and HJURP after centromeric transcript depletion, and citations to Barnhart et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The long-term loss of centromeric transcripts leads to mitotic defects.
source: The long-term loss of these centromeric transcripts leads to mitotic defects (Figure 6), which are physically underpinned by the loss of HJURP recruitment and CENP-A loading (Figure 7) to native centromeres.
evidence: Supported by mitotic cell IF data shown in Figure 6 and chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mitotic defects from loss of centromeric transcripts are physically underpinned by the loss of HJURP recruitment to native centromeres.
source: The long-term loss of these centromeric transcripts leads to mitotic defects (Figure 6), which are physically underpinned by the loss of HJURP recruitment and CENP-A loading (Figure 7) to native centromeres.
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mitotic defects from loss of centromeric transcripts are physically underpinned by the loss of CENP-A loading to native centromeres.
source: The long-term loss of these centromeric transcripts leads to mitotic defects (Figure 6), which are physically underpinned by the loss of HJURP recruitment and CENP-A loading (Figure 7) to native centromeres.
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 7.

claim: RNAPII and TBP are loaded onto and transcribe human centromeric chromatin at eG1.
source: We show that RNAPII and TBP are loaded onto and transcribe human centromeric chromatin at eG1 (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber IF and co-IP data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cell cycle regulated centromeric transcription is required for the synthesis of centromeric RNAs.
source: This cell cycle regulated centromeric transcription is required for the synthesis of centromeric RNAs (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by transcription inhibition experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Targeted destruction of centromeric RNA leads to the loss of centromere integrity.
source: Targeted destruction of this centromeric RNA leads to the loss of centromere integrity and subsequent mitotic and cellular defects (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Targeted destruction of centromeric RNA leads to subsequent mitotic defects.
source: Targeted destruction of this centromeric RNA leads to the loss of centromere integrity and subsequent mitotic and cellular defects (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Targeted destruction of centromeric RNA leads to subsequent cellular defects.
source: Targeted destruction of this centromeric RNA leads to the loss of centromere integrity and subsequent mitotic and cellular defects (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mitotic and cellular defects from centromeric RNA loss are mechanistically underpinned by the loss of HJURP recruitment to centromeres at eG1.
source: which are mechanistically underpinned by the loss of HJURP and CENP-A recruitment to centromeres at eG1 (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mitotic and cellular defects from centromeric RNA loss are mechanistically underpinned by the loss of CENP-A recruitment to centromeres at eG1.
source: which are mechanistically underpinned by the loss of HJURP and CENP-A recruitment to centromeres at eG1 (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The data reveal a hitherto unsuspected function for lncRNAs in RNA-dependent chaperone targeting to centromeres in human cells.
source: Altogether, these data reveal a hitherto unsuspected function for lncRNAs in RNA-dependent chaperone targeting to centromeres in human cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data showing RNA interaction with HJURP/CENP-A and requirement for centromere targeting.

claim: The repetitive nature of centromeric α-satellite DNA has thus far disallowed complete sequencing.
source: Because the repetitive nature of centromeric α-satellite DNA has thus far disallowed complete sequencing, successful annotation of transcriptional motifs that may exist in human centromeres remains to be accomplished.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the challenges of sequencing repetitive DNA.

claim: Successful annotation of transcriptional motifs that may exist in human centromeres remains to be accomplished.
source: Because the repetitive nature of centromeric α-satellite DNA has thus far disallowed complete sequencing, successful annotation of transcriptional motifs that may exist in human centromeres remains to be accomplished.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of complete sequencing of centromeric DNA.

claim: Centromeric transcription is an event integral to the epigenetic maintenance of centromere integrity.
source: Our data show that centromeric transcription is an event integral to the epigenetic maintenance of centromere integrity
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing requirement of transcription for CENP-A loading and centromere function.

claim: Previous data have shown that HJURP loading is dependent on its interaction with the Mis18 complex, in a CDK1-dependent manner.
source: We note that previous data have shown that HJURP loading is also dependent on its interaction with the Mis18 complex, in a CDK1-dependent manner (Barnhart et al., 2011; Moree et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barnhart et al., 2011; Moree et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations of CDK1-phosphorylated sites in HJURP only partially abrogate its recruitment in vivo.
source: However, mutations of CDK1-phosphorylated sites in HJURP only partially abrogate its recruitment in vivo, highlighting the existence of other hitherto unknown CENP-A loading factors (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Centromeric lncRNAs are the missing factor for CENP-A loading.
source: We speculate centromeric lncRNAs are, in fact, the missing factor.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Xist RNA binds its cognate DNA locus only in cis.
source: For example, whereas it is well known that Xist RNA binds its cognate DNA locus only in cis (Plath et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Plath et al., 2002.

claim: It is unknown if centromeric transcripts can bind in cis solely to the centromere of origin, or in trans, across all centromeres.
source: it is unknown if centromeric transcripts can bind in cis solely to the centromere of origin, or in trans, across all centromeres.
evidence: This is an open question based on the current state of knowledge.

claim: Centromeric RNAs may originate from multiple centromeres and serve a redundant function to ensure accurate targeting of CENP-A/HJURP to homologous centromeres.
source: An attractive possibility is centromeric RNAs originate from multiple centromeres and serve a redundant function to ensure accurate targeting of CENP-A/HJURP to homologous centromeres.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential mechanism.

claim: Prior studies have described RNA originating from centromeres in multiple species.
source: Prior studies have described RNA originating from centromeres in multiple species (Bouzinba-Segard et al., 2006; Carone et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouzinba-Segard et al., 2006; Carone et al., 2009.

claim: In mouse cells, a 120 nucleotide minor satellite RNA is associated with centromeres.
source: In mouse cells, a 120 nucleotide minor satellite RNA is associated with centromeres (Bouzinba-Segard et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bouzinba-Segard et al., 2006.

claim: In tammar wallaby, centromeric transcription results in the production of approximately 40 nucleotides crasiRNAs (centromere repeats-associated short interacting RNAs).
source: and in tammar wallaby, centromeric transcription results in the production of ∼40 nucleotides crasiRNAs (centromere repeats-associated short interacting RNAs) (Carone et al., 2009; Lindsay et al., 2012; Carone et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carone et al., 2009; Lindsay et al., 2012; Carone et al., 2013.

claim: The divergent nature of centromeric DNA sequences across species may lead to divergence in the type of centromeric RNAs produced.
source: A logical explanation for the difference in size of ncRNAs generated in different organisms may be the divergent nature of the centromeric DNA sequences across species, which in turn may lead to divergence in the type of centromeric RNAs produced.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain observed differences across species.

claim: Over-expression or down-regulation of mouse minor satellite RNA leads to cellular and mitotic defects.
source: However, despite this difference, over-expression or down-regulation of mouse minor satellite RNA, or crasiRNAs in tammar wallaby, or the 1.3 kb centromeric human RNA identified in our study, leads to similar cellular and mitotic defects.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with cited studies and data from this study.

claim: Over-expression or down-regulation of crasiRNAs in tammar wallaby leads to cellular and mitotic defects.
source: However, despite this difference, over-expression or down-regulation of mouse minor satellite RNA, or crasiRNAs in tammar wallaby, or the 1.3 kb centromeric human RNA identified in our study, leads to similar cellular and mitotic defects.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with cited studies and data from this study.

claim: Over-expression or down-regulation of the 1.3 kb centromeric human RNA leads to cellular and mitotic defects.
source: However, despite this difference, over-expression or down-regulation of mouse minor satellite RNA, or crasiRNAs in tammar wallaby, or the 1.3 kb centromeric human RNA identified in our study, leads to similar cellular and mitotic defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Mitotic loss seen in cells depleted of centromeric lncRNAs is specifically linked to abrogation of HJURP-mediated targeting of CENP-A.
source: Our data reveal that such RNAs generated from human centromeric transcription bind HJURP and CENP-A in the soluble form and that mitotic loss seen in cells depleted of these lncRNAs is specifically linked to abrogation of HJURP-mediated targeting of CENP-A.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing RNA binding to HJURP/CENP-A and loss of targeting upon RNA depletion.

claim: The data suggest an evolutionarily conserved basis for the phenomena of centromeric transcription seen in other organisms.
source: Thus, our data suggest an evolutionarily conserved basis for the phenomena of centromeric transcription seen in other organisms.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of centromeric RNA functions across species.

claim: Accurate CENP-A targeting onto active centromeres probably requires a dual-lock system, coupling chromatin-bound centromeric factors (such as Mis18) with a lncRNA/CENP-A/chaperone complex.
source: We speculate that accurate CENP-A targeting onto active centromeres probably requires a dual-lock system, coupling chromatin-bound centromeric factors (such as Mis18), which facilitate cell-cycle regulated centromeric transcription, which in turn results in the production of a lncRNA/CENP-A/chaperone complex that can effectively target CENP-A back to pre-existing active centromeric sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the combined data from this study and previous literature.

claim: Transcription-coupled, chaperone-mediated histone variant assembly governs much of chromatin biology.
source: It is noteworthy that transcription-coupled, chaperone-mediated histone variant assembly governs much of chromatin biology.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromatin biology.

claim: The report potentially reveals an RNA-based mechanism by which specialized histone-variant driven chromatin structures might be maintained in vivo.
source: Our report potentially reveals an RNA-based mechanism by which specialized histone-variant driven chromatin structures might be maintained in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing RNA involvement in CENP-A targeting.
